Buying 1896 Cedar Beach mansion — a historic no-brainer

Scooter MacMillan, Editor July 23, 2026July 22, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 11:52
Instaread

Alexa Lewis didn’t even make it into the mansion at Cedar Beach, that is now her home, before she had decided. Without hesitation, she told the real estate agent she wanted to buy it.

“We got as far as the porch. We were looking out over the water, and I just decided that it would do it for me,” Lewis said.

Lewis wasn’t the first to decide to buy the spacious mansion perched on a cliff overlooking Lake Champlain without entering the house itself.

In 1971, Katherine “Kit” Serrell walked onto the porch and, also without ever entering, reportedly told a real estate agent, “Wrap it up.”

The house, now known as the Pinnacle, was built in 1896 by William Van Patten, mayor of Burlington (1894-95) and a state senator (1906). During his sole term in the legislature, Van Patten served as Senate president.

The Pinnacle, which was known as Cedarcroft at that time, was the third camp Van Patten built at Cedar Beach in Charlotte. Until Lewis bought the Pinnacle, it had been used as a camp, but she winterized it. Now, it’s her home year-round.

During Van Patten’s time at Cedarcroft, he continued to work in Burlington while his family summered at the camp home at Cedar Beach. The Ticonderoga would pick him up at a dock there in the morning, and in the evening, the steamboat delivered him back to the camp.

In 1896, travel by horseback or carriage for work in Burlington would have been a difficult ride. In 1873, around 20 prominent Burlington families purchased land in the area, as the Jolly Club Camp. The only way for them to get to their vacation property was by boat because there was no road.

The name Jolly Club Camp only lasted about three years, because by 1876 it was being referred to as Cedar Beach. But there’s still a road at Cedar Beach named Jolly Camp Road.

Coming into adulthood during the Progressive Era, Van Patten was the embodiment of what his milieu’s moniker implies and more.

He moved to Burlington in 1864 and worked in the retail drug trade, then in wholesale. By 1872, he was a partner in Wells, Richardson and Company, a patent medicine firm that expanded into dyes and manufactured coloring for butter.

“His accomplishments over the next half century boggle the mind,” said Lillian Baker Carlisle in the “Chittenden County Historical Society Bulletin.”

Van Patten served presidencies for the Champlain Manufacturing Company, Malted Cereals, the Burlington Building and Loan Association, the Forestry Association of Vermont, the YMCA, the United Society of Christian Endeavor and the Burlington Commercial Club. He was on the boards of park, cemetery, library and hospital commissioners, the National Brotherhood of Congregational and World’s Christian Endeavor Union and a member of the Algonquin Club, the Vermont Fish and Game League, The Vermont Society of the Sons of the American Revolution and the Society of Colonial Wars.

During his mayoral term, he oversaw the city’s first paved streets and the creation of the first paid fire department.

Lewis’ impression is that the Thompson’s Point society of the Victorian era was mostly folks from Washington, D.C., who were used to much more formal dress and dining, while the Cedar Beach crowd was largely from the ranks of the “Boston Brahmin” and used to a tad less formal evening attire at their summer camps.

According to the April 1978 issue of the “Chittenden County Historical Society Bulletin,” in 1902, Van Patten bought portions of the Ethan Allen farm and property that became Ethan Allen Park for $20,000. He donated 12 acres to the Sons of the American Revolution for the park on the condition that a stone tower be erected there as a memorial to Allen. That tower was dedicated in 1905 — from a design by Van Patten.

Renovating her youngest house

The Pinnacle is the youngest house Lewis has ever owned. One of her previous homes was built in Massachusetts in 1730, around the corner from where Paul Revere would stay when he was going back and forth between Boston and the Cape on the Old Post Road, the first road ever built in that area.

Originally, Lewis bought property below Thompson’s Point, and she was going to build there until she realized: “I’m not a builder, I’m a renovator.”

After buying the Pinnacle in 2016 for around $1.1 million, she spent a couple of years figuring out how she was going to finance the renovations, which were extensive. It cost almost as much to renovate the house as buying it.

Lewis describes the renovation as “a big job,” which could win a gold medal if understatement was an Olympic event. The renovation work began just as the pandemic hit, so continuing required a lot of planning to cut down on the risk of spreading the virus.

There could only be two workers at a time, so it took two years to get the Pinnacle ready to be a full-time home.

She hired Neagley & Chase to handle the renovation work, but Lewis was on site working alongside the contractors, when she wasn’t commuting from a home she rented in Mallets Bay and Montpelier, where she was doing tax work for the state government. Lewis is very pleased with how the collaboration worked out and the result.

“The renovation was an exciting time,” Lewis said. It was not “saturated with stress” because Neagley & Chase had experience handling big projects like the Pinnacle. So, she could relax a little bit and enjoy the process because, as new issues turned up, they knew what do do.

“I really trusted my contractors. They really were wonderful,” Lewis said.

Among things that needed to be done: The kitchen needed to be completely gutted; mice had taken over. The kitchen floor had to be completely redone; it had been carpeted at some time in the past, a design choice that’s more typical of a summer camp than a year-round home. She added three bathrooms.

She had the iceboxes — yes, iceboxes — converted into modern refrigerators, but you can’t tell. The original doors were preserved, so it still looks like old-time iceboxes.

There were leaks in the ceiling that had to be fixed. Lewis had the walls, which originally had been wood, plastered, not sheet rocked.

The walls in the dining room were covered with woven black ash strips. This wall covering had deteriorated so much over the years that it needed to be replaced. But Lewis didn’t just fix it by tearing it down and applying wallpaper. Instead, she had workers who split wood into strips around an inch and half wide. They then wove lighter and darker strips as they put up the new wall covering to recreate the original.

Lewis acquired lots of furniture and other artifacts when she bought the Pinnacle. Almost all the door handles are original, and there are a few fixtures, preserved from a time when the lighting was gas, that were wired for electricity during the renovation.

Cyrus Wicker’s tenure

The Wickers changed the name of the camp to Eastwick. They had another camp to the west that was known as Westwick, so both camps’ names incorporated a portion of their last name, during a time long before there would be any confusion with “The Witches of Eastwick.”

Among artifacts she inherited from the house’s history is a set of Tibetan bells, which she assumes came from Cyrus Wicker’s tenure at the camp.

Wicker, who as a member of the diplomatic service, was a world traveler. He bought the Pinnacle from Van Patten in 1925 and owned it for 22 years until 1947.

He was stationed in Nicaragua and Panama. Lewis said that, between the World Wars, Wicker was very involved in bringing people together from all over the world for peace negotiations. Who knows who might have visited the Pinnacle — and from where?

One of Wicker’s sons, Cyrus French Wicker Jr., was killed in Myanmar, formerly Burma, during World War II. The fighting in Burma was brutal, but the younger Wicker was somewhat removed from the most dangerous areas as he served as a war photographer. He was assigned by the U.S. Army to British forces as they pushed south toward Rangoon.

However, Pfc. Wicker died on Memorial Day, May 30, 1945, just weeks after peace had been declared in the European theater but a few weeks before Japan surrendered, when his plane crashed during an emergency landing.

Lewis said she has heard Cyrus Wickers was so overcome by his son’s death that he pretty much abandoned the main house at the Pinnacle and stayed in the ice and carriage house on the property that he converted into a studio.

Renamed Pinnacle

Under the ownership of the Rev. Theodore Clapp the house became known as the Pinnacle.

During the early 1950s, while the Wickers still owned it, the house was empty and unlocked much of the time. Nancy Wood, the founder of this newspaper, remembers coming to the house with some older kids who had a dance party. Wood said she can’t remember much of that time, but she’s pretty sure the music was Glenn Miller and Louis Armstrong and probably early rock ‘n roll. Maybe instead of rockin’ around the clock, they may have been rockin’ around the dock.

Happy Patrick of the Charlotte Historical Society said she remembers going to the home with some older teenagers, who used the phone to make long-distance phone calls, possibly to keep the embers of distant young love glowing.

“Everybody’s got some memory or another of this place,” said Lewis.

The memories really accumulated under the Serrells, after Kit Serrell had instinctively recognized that this was the vacation spot for her family. When Cedar Beach held a centennial celebration with tours of various houses on the peninsula in the summer of 1983, she told the Burlington Free Press, “This is a house for an extended family, to provide roots for children who live all over the world.”

Kit Serrell’s husband Tim was a tennis pro who set up a fund in Charlotte for kids to learn tennis. And he was also a pilot. Lewis said, “He’s a pretty interesting guy.”

Their son Ted was a ferry captain on Lake Champlain, but he now lives in Florida. He sold the Pinnacle to Lewis.

In a 1983 Burlington Free Press story, Kit Serrell said the Pinnacle gave her descendants “roots in a very transient world.”

She proclaimed that she only had two rules she enforced with visiting grandchildren: “No daytime television, and I won’t take them to Burlington.”

When Lewis became the Pinnacle proprietor, it hadn’t been “camped” in for a few years and was mostly abandoned. In fact, it had been on the market for at least three years, but other potential buyers could see the amount of work needed was beyond their stamina or means.

The Pinnacle is still a good bit of a project. Even with all the work done to the walls, when the wind blows in winter, sometimes ornaments fall off Lewis’ Christmas tree.

“I think I heat the neighborhood,” she jokes. “It wasn’t really made for year-round living, and we do the best we can.”

Lewis says it is still a great summer house. It is a lot of house for one person, but she doesn’t get lonely; she loves to entertain.
